cards.explanation: The answer is thirty-eight years. John 5:5 says this man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. That's a long stretch of years to live with that condition. Hold onto that number, friends, because it makes what happens next hit even harder.

The answer is “Do you want to get well?” (John 5:6). After thirty-eight years, Jesus starts with a question instead of a speech. I think that's a kind way to begin a talk with someone who's been lying there so long.

The problem is that he has no one to help him in. He tells Jesus, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred.” (John 5:7). He adds that while he is on his way, someone else goes in before him. I think there's a lot of weight in that answer, friends.
Jesus tells him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” (John 5:8). No pool, no waiting, no one racing him to the water. Jesus just speaks, and that's all it takes.
The answer is False. John 5:9 says, “Immediately the man was made well…” No waiting around and no gradual improvement. After thirty-eight years, he picked up his mat and began to walk.

The word is carry. The Jews tell him, “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” (John 5:10). They don't say a word about the miracle. They go straight to the mat. I'd have been asking, “Wait, how are you WALKING?”

The word is well. The healed man answers, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’…” (John 5:11). His point is simple: the man who made him well is the one who told him to do it. That's the answer he gives the Jews.

The reason is that Jesus had slipped away in the crowd. John 5:13 says the healed man did not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. He got healed, and the one who healed him was already gone. I think that's a head-scratcher, friends, and I've never been so quietly vanished on.

The answer is True. Jesus finds him at the temple and says, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” (John 5:14). That's a serious word, and I think it's said with care. Jesus went and found him, and that matters.

The answer is False. John 5:15 says the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. When they asked him earlier, he did not know who it was (John 5:12-13). Now he names Jesus to the Jews.

Jesus answers, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” (John 5:17). He doesn't back up. He points to His Father and says He's working too. That sets up everything He says next, friends.

The answer is False. John 5:18 says, “Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.” Two things, and the text names both. The Sabbath was only part of it.

The answer is False. Jesus says, “…the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does.” (John 5:19). He's not working alone. The Father and the Son are doing the same work together.

The answer is True. Jesus says, “…just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.” (John 5:21). Giving life to the dead is no small thing. That's a claim big enough to shake a chef's hat right off.

The reason is so all may honor the Son like the Father. Jesus says the Father has assigned all judgment to the Son “…so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” (John 5:22-23). Then He adds that whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him. The two go together, friends. You can't skip one and keep the other.

The word is life. Jesus says whoever hears His word and believes Him who sent Him “…has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.” (John 5:24). Crossed over, friends. Death on one side, life on the other.

The answer is False. Jesus says “all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28-29). Those who have done good come out to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. Nobody gets left out of the hearing.

His judgment is just because He seeks the will of the One who sent Him. Jesus says, “…My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.” (John 5:30). He also says, “I judge only as I hear.” So His judgment rests on the will of the One who sent Him, not on His own will.

The answer is False. Jesus says, “There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid.” (John 5:32). He isn't standing alone. And He's about to list who stands with Him.

The picture is a lamp that burned and gave light. Jesus says, “John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light.” (John 5:35). A lamp burns and gives light for others to see by. And He says they were willing to bask in it, for a season.

The testimony is the works the Father gave Him to do. Jesus says the works the Father has given Him to accomplish, the very works He is doing, testify that the Father has sent Him (John 5:36). The works speak, friends. That includes the man who got up and walked at Bethesda.

The answer is someone who comes in his own name. Jesus says, “I have come in My Father’s name, and you have not received Me; but if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him.” (John 5:43). It's a sharp line. Jesus comes in the Father's name and isn't received, while someone coming in his own name would be.

The answer is Moses. Jesus says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one they trusted. And Jesus goes on to say that Moses wrote about Him, friends.
